lead: Logical effort is a hand calculation that predicts the delay of a logic path before you size transistors. It separates a gate's topology cost (logical effort g and parasitic delay p) from its load (electrical effort h). Multiplying stage efforts gives a path effort F. For a fixed load and a fixed number of stages, delay is smallest when every stage carries the same effort. The result tells you how wide to make each transistor. Cell designers, synthesis tools and students checking a timing budget use it when a quick estimate is more useful than a full SPICE run.
prereq: You need Chapter 3.3 for propagation delay and load capacitance.

sections.h3: The delay model for one gate

blocks.text: A logic gate drives capacitance through transistors that have finite on-resistance. Chapter 3.3 called the result propagation delay. Logical effort writes that delay in units of τ. A reference inverter with no external load has delay τ. Driving an identical inverter, it has delay 2τ in this model. The model has two parts: a load-dependent part and a fixed part.

The electrical effort h = C<sub>out</sub>/C<sub>in</sub>. C<sub>out</sub> is the total capacitance at the gate output, in farads. C<sub>in</sub> is the capacitance looking into the gate input, in farads. h is dimensionless and is also called fanout. The logical effort g is dimensionless. It compares the input capacitance of the gate with an inverter that can deliver the same output current. A gate with large g needs more input capacitance for the same drive. The parasitic delay p is the delay with no external load, in τ units. It comes from the gate's own diffusion capacitance.
d = (g h + p) τ = (f + p) τ
blocks.where: d is the stage delay in seconds; τ is the reference inverter delay in seconds; g is logical effort (dimensionless); h = C<sub>out</sub>/C<sub>in</sub> is electrical effort (dimensionless); p is parasitic delay in τ units; f = g h is stage effort (dimensionless).

blocks.text: These numbers assume equal rise and fall times and a symmetric inverter. The inverter is the reference: g=1, p=1. A 2-input NAND has g=4/3, p=2. A 2-input NOR has g=5/3, p=2. Series nMOS transistors make the NAND slower and wider; the NOR is worse because its series pMOS transistors are weaker.

sections.h3: Equal stage effort and transistor sizing

blocks.text: Consider a path of N gates from an input capacitance C<sub>in,path</sub> to an output load C<sub>out,path</sub>. The path logical effort G = Π g<sub>i</sub>. The path electrical effort H = C<sub>out,path</sub>/C<sub>in,path</sub>. If a node drives extra gates off the path, include branch effort b = (C<sub>on</sub> + C<sub>off</sub>)/C<sub>on</sub>, where C<sub>on</sub> is capacitance on the path and C<sub>off</sub> is capacitance off the path. The path branch effort B = Π b<sub>i</sub>. The path effort F = G B H. With no branches B=1.

The path delay in τ units is D = Σ f<sub>i</sub> + Σ p<sub>i</sub>. For fixed F and N, the arithmetic mean–geometric mean inequality says Σ f<sub>i</sub> is smallest when all f<sub>i</sub> equal. Set each stage effort to f = F<sup>1/N</sup>. Then D = N f + P, where P = Σ p<sub>i</sub>.
F = G B H, f = F<sup>1/N</sup>, D = N f + P
blocks.where: F is path effort; G = Π g<sub>i</sub>; B = Π b<sub>i</sub>; H = C<sub>out,path</sub>/C<sub>in,path</sub>; N is number of stages; f is equal stage effort; P = Σ p<sub>i</sub>; D is path delay in τ units.

items: List the gates in order and the load capacitance at each node.
Compute G = product of g values; H = C<sub>out,path</sub>/C<sub>in,path</sub>; B = product of b values.
Compute F = G B H; N = number of stages; f = F<sup>1/N</sup>.
Work backward from the load. For stage i, C<sub>in,i</sub> = g<sub>i</sub> C<sub>out,i</sub>/f, where C<sub>out,i</sub> is the total capacitance driven by that stage.
Set transistor widths in proportion to C<sub>in,i</sub>. For equal channel length, W scales with capacitance.

blocks.text: This is path delay optimisation; some syllabi call it the method of logical effort. It gives first-pass sizes. A static timing tool refines them.

figure.caption: The NAND2 line has intercept 2τ at h=0 and rises with slope 4/3; the inverter intercept is 1τ and slope 1. At h=1 the delays are 3.33τ and 2τ. The vertical gap is the topology cost before load is added.

spec.aria: Two straight lines: NAND2 has a higher intercept and a steeper slope than an inverter.

examples.question: A path has three stages: INV → NAND2 → INV. Its final load is 64 times the input capacitance C of a minimum inverter. Ignore branches and use the standard values in this chapter. Find G, H, F, N, f, P and D. Also find the input capacitance of each stage relative to C when the path is sized for equal stage effort.
steps: The three stages are INV, NAND2 and INV, so N = 3. From the table, G = g<sub>INV</sub> × g<sub>NAND2</sub> × g<sub>INV</sub> = 1 × 4/3 × 1 = 4/3 ≈ 1.333.
The path input capacitance is C and the final load is 64C, so H = 64C/C = 64. There are no branches, so B = 1.
The path effort is F = G B H = (4/3) × 1 × 64 = 256/3 ≈ 85.33.
The equal stage effort is f = F<sup>1/3</sup> = (85.33)<sup>1/3</sup> = 4.4026 ≈ 4.40.
The total parasitic delay is P = p<sub>INV</sub> + p<sub>NAND2</sub> + p<sub>INV</sub> = 1 + 2 + 1 = 4τ.

Work backward for sizing. Last INV: C<sub>in3</sub> = g C<sub>out</sub>/f = 1 × 64C/4.4026 = 14.54C. NAND2: C<sub>in2</sub> = (4/3) × 14.54C/4.4026 = 4.40C. First INV: C<sub>in1</sub> = 1 × 4.40C/4.4026 = 1.00C.
examples.answer: The path delay is about 17.2τ, and the NAND2 input capacitance is about 4.40C; the last inverter input is about 14.54C and the first inverter input is about 1.00C.
examples.check:
import math
G = 1 * (4/3) * 1
H = 64
N = 3
F = G * H
f = F ** (1/3)
P = 1 + 2 + 1
D = N * f + P
Cin3 = 64 / f
Cin2 = (4/3) * Cin3 / f
Cin1 = Cin2 / f
print(round(G, 3))
print(H)
print(round(F, 2))
print(N)
print(round(f, 2))
print(P)
print(round(D, 1))
print(round(Cin3, 2))
print(round(Cin2, 2))
print(round(Cin1, 2))

traps: Forgetting branch effort b at a node that fans out to two paths makes F too small and the path look faster than it is.
Mixing up g and p: g multiplies fanout, while p is a constant intercept. A NAND2 has larger p (2τ) than an inverter (1τ).
Using H = C<sub>input</sub>/C<sub>load</sub> instead of C<sub>load</sub>/C<sub>input</sub>. H is output load divided by path input capacitance.
Multiplying P by N, or adding P after already using it inside every stage, double-counts parasitic delay. P = Σ p<sub>i</sub> is added once to N f.
Sizing every gate to the same width. Equal stage effort usually means different input capacitances; the NAND2 in the example is about 4.40 times a minimum inverter.

quiz.q: Define logical effort g, parasitic delay p and electrical effort h.
quiz.a: g is the input capacitance of a gate relative to an inverter with the same output current, dimensionless. p is the delay with zero external load, in τ units. h = C<sub>out</sub>/C<sub>in</sub> is the electrical effort or fanout, dimensionless.

quiz.q: Why is a 2-input NAND's logical effort greater than 1?
quiz.a: For the same output current, the series nMOS stack forces each nMOS to be wider; that extra gate capacitance raises the input capacitance to 4/3 of the reference inverter. The parallel pMOS need not be wider than the inverter pMOS.

quiz.q: An inverter drives a load of 16 C, where C is its own input capacitance. Using d = f + p, find its delay in τ units.
quiz.a: h = C<sub>out</sub>/C<sub>in</sub> = 16C/C = 16. f = g h = 1 × 16 = 16. p = 1τ. d = 16 + 1 = 17τ.

quiz.q: A path has G = 2, H = 32, B = 1, N = 4 and P = 5τ. Find F, f and D.
A path has delay 20τ, N = 3 and P = 5τ. What equal stage effort does the model imply? If G = 1 and B = 1, what H is needed?
Why does equal stage effort minimise path delay?
quiz.a: For fixed path effort F and N stages, the product of stage efforts is fixed. By AM-GM, the sum of stage efforts is smallest when all stage efforts are equal. One oversized stage raises the sum and wastes delay.

quiz.q: Give g and p for an inverter, a 2-input NAND and a 2-input NOR.
quiz.a: INV: g = 1, p = 1τ. NAND2: g = 4/3, p = 2τ. NOR2: g = 5/3, p = 2τ.

quiz.q: A node drives 3C of on-path capacitance and 1C of off-path capacitance. Find its branch effort b.

beyond: Not for the exam. Logical effort is the basis of fanout optimisation in synthesis and of many cell libraries' drive-strength tables. Modern tools combine it with Elmore delay, slew and interconnect RC. FinFET and multi-V<sub>t</sub> libraries add more g and p values. Search terms: logical effort, path delay optimisation, fanout-of-four inverter, drive strength selection.
